sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Kaiserreich
sources.note: 1871-1918 German Empire overview, constitutional monarchy, industrialization, 1918 defeat and end; overview is retrospective.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Reichsgründung 1871
sources.note: January 1871 imperial unification in Franco-Prussian War setting; federal continuities and flag, not an empty-land foundation.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Reichsverfassung 1871
sources.note: 1871 constitutional monarchy, emperor, Bundesrat, elected Reichstag and limits of parliamentary power.

sources.title: Historical German constitutional law transcription, Gesetz betreffend die Verfassung des Deutschen Reiches 1871
sources.note: Transcription of contemporary 1871 Reich law begins Wir Wilhelm, von Gottes Gnaden Deutscher Kaiser; short German sample taken from this text. This is a historical law transcription, not a facsimile.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Alltagsleben im Kaiserreich
sources.note: Industrial city tenements versus wealthy homes, women's family earnings, sanitation and water networks, medical progress, changing work and leisure; context varies by class and region.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Sozialgesetzgebung
sources.note: 1883 workers health insurance, 1884 accident, 1889 old age/disability laws; partial scope and labor criticism.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Frauenbewegung
sources.note: Women organized for education, employment and political rights; 1894 umbrella group, 1908 association/party membership rights, no imperial women's vote.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Wissenschaft und Forschung
sources.note: Research and technical development, 1911 Kaiser Wilhelm Society, differing gymnasium/realschule curricula and regular female matriculation at Prussian universities 1908-09.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Reformzeit um 1900
sources.note: Citizens' and women's associations campaigned for child-centered education, better housing, hygiene, nature protection and peace; varied aims, not a single movement.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, Antisemiten-Petition
sources.note: Antisemitic campaign from 1870s against Jewish civic equality despite legal emancipation; prejudice persisted in public politics.

sources.title: Robert Koch Institute, Robert Koch
sources.note: Koch announced tuberculosis pathogen discovery in Berlin 24 March 1882; medical advance did not instantly cure patients.

sources.title: Berlin Senate, Chronology of Public Toilets
sources.note: Berlin first two public urinals 1863, octagonal cast-iron pissoirs planned from 1878, women-and-men public toilets around 1900; capital-specific.

sources.title: Berlin Senate, Expansion of the City
sources.note: Berlin commissioned Hobrecht sewerage expansion in 1873 against dangerous street wastewater; capital-specific infrastructure.

sources.title: Berlin state history, The Imperial Capital
sources.note: 1903 Berlin housing survey: many one- or two-room apartments amid growth; local city housing evidence.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, German South West Africa
sources.note: Colonial rule and Herero/Nama resistance, mass deaths, deliberate starvation/dehydration, camps and land seizure 1904-08; museum account.

sources.title: German Federal Archives, War against the Herero 1904
sources.note: Federal Archives names genocide of the Herero during German colonial war and concentration camps; survivors continued.

sources.title: Deutsches Historisches Museum, First World War Everyday Life
sources.note: 1914-18 war transformed family work and food supply, rationing, turnip winter 1916-17 and undernutrition; loss varied by class.

sources.title: German Federal Archives, Proclamation of the Republic 9 November 1918
sources.note: Kiel sailors' revolt spread to Berlin; emperor's abdication announced and republic proclaimed 9 November 1918. Empire political end distinct from continued people/culture.

sources.title: House of Austrian History, 1867 Dual Monarchy and Basic Rights
sources.note: 1867 Ausgleich created dual monarchy with separate Austrian and Hungarian structures under common monarch; December constitution applied to Austrian half.

sources.title: House of Austrian History, Multilingualism and Diversity
sources.note: Habsburg Monarchy had nine official languages, varied communities; successor states created after 1918.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, Problems and Potentialities of a Multiethnic State
sources.note: More than ten spoken languages, unequal political influence after Ausgleich, Slavic demands for autonomy; interpretive museum essay.

sources.title: House of Austrian History, Czech School Association Collection Tin
sources.note: Vienna Czech community began organizing own-language vocational education in 1868 and raising funds; one language community and city, not empire-wide.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, Language and Nationality Policies
sources.note: Different school language policies in Austrian and Hungarian halves; language rights in law differed from practice.

sources.title: Austrian Legal Information System, 1867 Basic Law Article 19
sources.note: Official Austrian legal text: Alle Volksstämme des Staates sind gleichberechtigt; a short German-language sample from Austrian-half 1867 rights law, not a claim that all subjects used German or equality was realized.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, Nuclear Family as Luxury Commodity
sources.note: Around 1900 working families sometimes occupied one room and kitchen and relied on Bettgeher bed-tenants or women's earnings; social-class and urban specificity.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, The Emperor and his Valet
sources.note: Memoir-based elite court vignette: valet Ketterl, 14 chamber staff, emperor's pot and Schönbrunn lavatory; memoir viewpoint is partial.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, Running Water in Vienna
sources.note: Vienna 1873 Alpine water pipeline, 1910 second line, contaminated groundwater and uneven inner/outer district household bathrooms and toilets.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, Mobility in Film
sources.note: Railway, trams, bicycles, early cars and films around 1900; estimated 300,000-400,000 bicycles and annual production, with locality/access limits.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, The 1908 Annexation Crisis
sources.note: Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied from 1878 and annexed in 1908, causing diplomatic crisis; political control was contested.

sources.title: The World of the Habsburgs, Ringstrasse Architecture
sources.note: Vienna Ringstrasse civic buildings as historicist urban design; capital construction not representative of provincial housing.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, School Front
sources.note: 1914-18 schoolchildren involved in propaganda, essays and drawing; specific wartime schooling, not all children equally.

sources.title: House of Austrian History, School Closures During Epidemics
sources.note: Edelsbach school headteacher wrote of recurring childhood illness in 1898; retrospective account discusses closures during 1918 epidemics and later decades.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, Vienna as Centre of War Economy
sources.note: Food shortages, women's work, queues, soup kitchens in wartime Vienna; city/war-period evidence.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, Playing with Fire
sources.note: Sarajevo assassination 28 June 1914 and separate government decisions toward war; causation not treated as automatic.

sources.title: The First World War exhibition, Last Days of the Monarchy
sources.note: Autumn 1918 collapse, 3 November demobilization, Charles/Karl renounced participation in state affairs 11 November, no single successor to all lands.

proposedOverrides.summary: The German Empire united German states under a Prussian king as emperor in 1871. It grew into an industrial and scientific power, but class divisions, colonial violence and political exclusions shaped its rule. Workers and families lived far from the palace image. Defeat and revolution ended the imperial monarchy in 1918; German people and communities continued.

proposedOverrides.summary: Austria-Hungary formed a dual monarchy in 1867 under the Habsburg ruler. Its many languages and communities, two governments, cities and countryside made it more than a single culture. Daily life ranged from crowded workers' rooms to multilingual schools and court service. War and competing national movements brought the monarchy to an end in 1918; its peoples and traditions continued.
